Upon hatching, these young individuals possess a snout-vent length of roughly 2.58 centimeters [Lb = roughly 2.58 centimeters], a modest starting size that reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development within a cleidoic egg. Their initial body mass is equally slight, with wet weight at birth averaging 0.46 grams [Wwb = 0.46 grams], a value that underscores the necessity of rapid growth and early exogenous feeding to escape the vulnerability window characteristic of juvenile reptiles in alpine environments. This life-history strategy, common among high-elevation lacertids, prioritizes a relatively brief embryonic phase to align hatching with the short summer window of the Pyrenean peaks.

Growth proceeds steadily during the juvenile phase, with the first reproductive milestone appearing after a well-defined period. Under the cool thermal regime typical of the species' subalpine habitat, 14 °C [T = 14 °C], females attain puberty at a time since birth of approximately 1642.5 days [tp = approximately 1642.5 days]. This prolonged pre-reproductive juvenile stage, equivalent to roughly 4.5 years, is a direct consequence of the low metabolic rates sustained at such temperatures. Males mature slightly earlier, reaching sexual maturation after about 1642.5 days since birth [tp = about 1642.5 days since birth] as well, but at a smaller body dimension at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. Females, which must accommodate a clutch of eggs within their body cavity, reach a maximum recorded SVL of 6.54 centimeters [Li = 6.54 centimeters]. Males, by contrast, achieve a slightly smaller ultimate SVL of 5.87 centimeters [Li = 5.87 centimeters], a difference commonly observed in oviparous reptiles where fecundity selection operates more strongly on female body volume. The ultimate wet weight of these breeding individuals, independent of sex, has been documented at 5.12 grams [Wwi = 5.12 grams], representing a more than tenfold increase from the 0.46 grams [Wwb = 0.46 grams] recorded at the hatching event. This substantial mass gain is accomplished over the course of several years of continuous feeding and somatic growth.

Longevity in this species is constrained by the same thermal environment that governs its developmental pace. Field records indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] when individuals are maintained under the thermal conditions approximating their natural active-season temperatures, specifically 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This remarkable longevity, unusually high for a small-bodied lacertid, is made possible by the species' slow metabolic rate and low predation pressure in its high-altitude talus slope refuges. The extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, a critical life-history adaptation given the short annual activity window in which the post-pubertal adult must locate mates, produce a clutch, and ensure the incubation of eggs before winter snowfall. Senescence appears to be gradual, with no abrupt post-reproductive decline in body condition.

Reproductive investment in this oviparous adult is paced by the constraints of the alpine climate. The initiation of reproductive activity, corresponding to the age at which gravid individuals are first observed in the field, occurs after a prolonged period that mirrors the timing of puberty. First reproduction events in females align closely with approximately 1642.5 days since birth [tp = approximately 1642.5 days since birth], although some individuals may delay their first egg clutch by an additional season if body condition is suboptimal at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. The relatively late onset of breeding, combined with a maximum lifespan of roughly 16 years [am = roughly 16 years] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], means that the reproductive window is limited to perhaps a decade of potential clutches. This life-history strategy, emphasizing delayed maturity and extended iteroparity, is typical of lizards adapted to cold, unproductive mountain ecosystems.
